scenario: Which statement best describes Linux?

options.text: A kernel; a full operating system (a distribution) combines it with tools, libraries, and applications
A complete operating system made by one company
options.note: Linux distributions come from many projects and vendors.
GNOME and KDE Plasma are desktop environments.
Linux is written mostly in C, but it isn't a language.

explanation: Linux is the kernel: the core that manages hardware and processes. A distribution adds GNU tools, libraries, a package manager and applications to make a usable operating system. No single company makes 'Linux', and it isn't a desktop or a language.

scenario: Which pair of distributions both belong to the Debian family and use .deb packages?

options.note: These are Red Hat family distributions using RPM.
Both are RHEL rebuilds that use RPM.

explanation: Ubuntu and Linux Mint are Debian-family distributions that use .deb packages and apt. Fedora and RHEL (also Rocky and AlmaLinux) are the Red Hat family using .rpm and dnf, and openSUSE/SLES use RPM with zypper.

scenario: Which distribution is the upstream development platform for Red Hat Enterprise Linux?

options.note: Arch is an independent rolling-release distribution.

explanation: Fedora is upstream of RHEL: new technology lands in Fedora, then CentOS Stream, which tracks just ahead of the next RHEL minor release. Rocky and AlmaLinux are downstream rebuilds, not upstream.

scenario: A company needs a Linux distribution with paid vendor support and long-term updates for its servers. Which choice fits best?

options.text: An enterprise distribution such as RHEL or SUSE Linux Enterprise Server

options.note: Rolling releases change constantly and usually lack commercial support.
Live media is for testing or recovery.

explanation: Servers that need paid vendor support and long update lifetimes call for an enterprise distribution such as RHEL or SUSE Linux Enterprise Server (Ubuntu LTS with Canonical support also fits). Rolling-release hobbyist distributions change constantly.

scenario: What does LTS mean for a release such as Ubuntu 24.04 LTS?

options.text: Long-term support: security and maintenance updates for an extended period

options.note: LTS releases are stable, not test builds.
LTS releases are available for desktops too.

explanation: LTS means long-term support: Ubuntu LTS releases arrive every two years and get five years of standard security and maintenance updates, longer with Ubuntu Pro. It is not a test snapshot or server-only.

scenario: Which open source application is a full office suite with a word processor, spreadsheet, and presentation program?
explanation: LibreOffice is the open source office suite: Writer (documents), Calc (spreadsheets) and Impress (presentations). GIMP edits images, Thunderbird is email and Blender is 3D.

scenario: Which program is an open source web server?

options.note: Postfix is a mail transfer agent.

explanation: Apache HTTP Server (httpd) and NGINX are the common open source web servers. MariaDB is a database, Samba shares files with Windows, and Postfix is a mail server.

scenario: Which software lets Linux servers share files and printers with Windows clients using SMB?

options.note: NFS is native Unix/Linux file sharing.
CUPS is the print system, not Windows file sharing.

explanation: Samba implements the SMB/CIFS protocol so Linux can share files and printers with Windows clients, and can even act as an Active Directory domain controller. NFS is the Unix-native file sharing protocol and CUPS handles printing.

scenario: What is the defining feature of a copyleft license such as the GNU GPL?

options.text: Anyone who distributes modified versions must release them under the same license with source code
The software can never be sold
Source code must be kept secret

explanation: A copyleft license such as the GPL requires that distributed modified versions stay under the same license with source available. Copyleft software can still be sold and used commercially. Permissive licenses don't impose that rule.

refs.title: The Open Source Definition - Open Source Initiative

scenario: Which license is permissive rather than copyleft?

options.note: AGPL is copyleft, extended to network use.
LGPL is weak copyleft for libraries.

explanation: The MIT License is permissive: it requires attribution but lets derivatives be closed source. GPL, AGPL and LGPL are copyleft to varying degrees.

refs.title: The Open Source Definition - Open Source Initiative

scenario: What does "free" mean in the Free Software Foundation's definition of free software?

options.text: Freedom to run, study, change, and share the software

options.note: "Free as in speech, not as in beer."
Free software is copyrighted and licensed.

explanation: In free software, 'free' means freedom (as in speech): to run, study and change, redistribute and distribute modified copies. It isn't about price, bug-free code or copyright status.

refs.title: The Open Source Definition - Open Source Initiative

scenario: Which organization approves licenses as meeting the Open Source Definition?

options.note: It hosts projects but doesn't approve licenses.
The FSF maintains the free software definition and GPL.

explanation: The Open Source Initiative maintains the Open Source Definition and approves licenses that meet it (GPL, MIT, Apache 2.0, BSD, MPL). The FSF defines free software separately, and the Linux Foundation is a different organization.

refs.title: The Open Source Definition - Open Source Initiative

scenario: Which business model is common for companies built on open source software?

options.text: Selling support subscriptions, services, training, and hosted versions
Charging license fees for the source code
options.note: Open source code is freely available.

explanation: Open source companies typically sell support subscriptions, certified updates, training, services and hosted versions (Red Hat, SUSE, Canonical). They can't charge for source code or hide it under copyleft terms.

scenario: Which statement about running Linux in the cloud is correct?

options.text: Most cloud instances run Linux images that are provisioned automatically, often with cloud-init
Linux can't run in public clouds
options.note: Linux is the most common cloud OS.

options.text: Cloud instances must be installed from DVD
Each cloud instance needs its own physical server
options.note: Instances are virtual machines on shared hosts.

explanation: Most cloud Linux instances start from a provider-supplied image of Ubuntu, RHEL, Debian or SUSE, and cloud-init configures hostname, users and SSH keys at first boot. There is no installer DVD or per-instance physical server.

scenario: What is a container compared with a virtual machine?

options.text: An isolated set of processes sharing the host's kernel, with its own filesystem image
A full guest OS with its own kernel on a hypervisor

explanation: A container is an isolated set of processes sharing the host kernel with its own filesystem image, so it is lighter and faster to start than a VM. A virtual machine runs a complete guest OS and kernel on a hypervisor. Podman and Docker are container tools.

scenario: What is Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL)?

options.text: A Windows feature that runs Linux distributions and their command-line tools on Windows
A Linux desktop that looks like Windows
A file system for USB drives

explanation: WSL lets you run Linux distributions and command-line tools directly on Windows; WSL 2 uses a real Linux kernel in a lightweight VM. It isn't an emulator, a Linux desktop or a file system.

refs.title: What is the Windows Subsystem for Linux?

scenario: Which program is a desktop environment rather than an application?

options.note: Inkscape is a vector graphics editor.

explanation: KDE Plasma is a desktop environment, as are GNOME, Xfce and Cinnamon; they sit on top of a display server such as Wayland or X11. Firefox, VLC and Inkscape are applications that run inside it.

scenario: Which programming languages are commonly used to write scripts and tools on Linux?

options.note: C is used for the kernel, but scripting languages are common.
Java is used but isn't the main scripting choice.
PowerShell runs on Linux but isn't the traditional choice.

explanation: Bash for shell scripts, Python for automation and tools, and Perl are all common on Linux, while C remains the kernel's language. Linux isn't tied to a single scripting language.

scenario: What is a strong password practice for a Linux user?

options.text: Use a long, unique passphrase per account, stored in a password manager, with MFA where available

options.note: One breach then exposes every account.

options.text: Write passwords on a sticky note
Use your username as your password

explanation: Use a long, unique passphrase per account, keep them in a password manager and add multi-factor authentication where possible. Reusing a password everywhere means one breach exposes everything.

scenario: When should you prefer an encrypted protocol such as SSH or HTTPS?

options.text: Whenever credentials or private data cross a network
Only on the internet, never on a LAN
options.note: Internal networks can be sniffed too.

explanation: Use encrypted protocols (SSH, SFTP/SCP, HTTPS) whenever credentials or private data cross a network, including internal LANs. Telnet and FTP send everything, including passwords, in plaintext.

scenario: Which command shows the full path of your current working directory?
explanation: pwd prints the full path of the current working directory, for example /home/alex/projects. cd changes directory, ls lists, and whoami prints your user name.

scenario: You type: cd ~ . Where do you end up?
explanation: The tilde (~) expands to your home directory, so cd ~ takes you there; plain cd with no argument does too. The root directory is /, and cd - returns to the previous directory.

scenario: Which path is absolute?
explanation: An absolute path starts at the root (/), so /etc/ssh/sshd_config is absolute. Relative paths start from the working directory, where . is the current directory and .. is its parent.

scenario: Which command lists all files, including hidden ones, in long format?
explanation: ls -la combines -a (include hidden files whose names start with a dot) and -l (long format with permissions, owner, size and date). -h only makes sizes human-readable and -R recurses.

scenario: How do you get detailed documentation for the ls command?

options.note: help covers Bash builtins; ls is an external program.

explanation: man ls opens the manual page for ls. info shows GNU info documents, command --help gives a short summary, and help covers shell builtins like cd. There is no ls --manual.

scenario: Which man page section contains configuration file formats, such as passwd(5)?
explanation: Section 5 of the manual covers file formats and configuration files, so man 5 passwd describes /etc/passwd, while man 1 passwd documents the command. Section 8 is system administration commands.

scenario: You don't remember the command for a task. Which command searches man page descriptions for a keyword?

options.note: whatis gives one-line descriptions of known names.
which finds an executable in PATH.

explanation: apropos (the same as man -k) searches the names and short descriptions of all manual pages for a keyword. which and locate find files and executables, not documentation.

scenario: Which command shows the location of the executable that runs when you type python3?
explanation: which python3 searches the directories in $PATH and shows the executable that would run. type is similar but also reports whether a name is a builtin, alias or file.

scenario: What does the PATH environment variable contain?

options.text: A colon-separated list of directories the shell searches for commands

explanation: PATH is a colon-separated list of directories the shell searches for commands, for example /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin. Add one with export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/bin". It isn't the current directory.

scenario: How do you set a variable so programs started from the shell can see it?

options.note: Spaces around = are a syntax error in Bash.
set alone doesn't create an exported variable.

explanation: VAR=value creates a shell variable, and export VAR=value (or export VAR afterwards) makes it an environment variable that child processes inherit. Spaces around = break the assignment.

scenario: What is the difference between single and double quotes in Bash?

options.text: Double quotes allow variable expansion; single quotes keep everything literal
Single quotes expand variables; double quotes don't
Only double quotes can contain spaces

explanation: Double quotes allow variable and command expansion, while single quotes keep everything literal. echo "$HOME" prints /home/alex but echo '$HOME' prints $HOME. Both can contain spaces.

scenario: Which command creates the nested directories projects/2026/reports in one step?

options.note: Fails if the parent directories don't exist.

explanation: mkdir -p creates all missing parent directories in one command and doesn't complain if the directory already exists. Without -p, mkdir fails when a parent is missing.

scenario: How do you copy the directory photos and everything in it to /backup?
explanation: cp -r (or -R) copies a directory and its contents recursively; without it cp refuses to copy a directory. -a also preserves permissions, ownership and timestamps.

scenario: Which command renames report.txt to report-old.txt?
explanation: mv moves or renames, so mv report.txt report-old.txt renames the file. cp would leave the original in place, and rn is not a standard command.

scenario: Which command deletes an empty directory named old?
explanation: rmdir removes only empty directories. rm old fails on a directory, while rm -r removes a directory and everything in it, so be careful.

scenario: What does ls *.log match in the current directory?

options.text: Every non-hidden file whose name ends in .log

explanation: * matches any characters, so ls *.log lists every non-hidden file ending in .log in the current directory only. The shell expands the glob before ls runs, and * does not match leading dots or descend into subdirectories.

scenario: Which glob matches file1.txt, file2.txt, and file3.txt but not file10.txt?
explanation: ? matches exactly one character, so file?.txt matches file1.txt through file3.txt but not file10.txt, which has two characters. file*.txt would match file10.txt too.

scenario: What does the command history | tail -5 show?

options.text: The last five commands you ran
The last five lines of every log

explanation: history lists your previous commands (stored in ~/.bash_history), and tail -5 keeps the last five lines of that output. !! reruns the last command and Ctrl+R searches history.

scenario: Which key completes a partially typed command or file name in Bash?

options.note: Ctrl+D sends end-of-file or logs out.

explanation: Tab completes a partially typed command or file name; press it twice to list the possibilities. Ctrl+C interrupts and Ctrl+D ends input.

scenario: What is the difference between a hard link and a symbolic link?

options.text: A hard link is another name for the same inode; a symbolic link is a pointer to a path

options.note: They behave differently when the original is deleted.

options.text: Symbolic links can't point to directories
Hard links work across file systems
options.note: Hard links must stay on the same file system.

explanation: A hard link is another directory entry for the same inode, so it survives deletion of the original name. A symbolic link stores a path and breaks if the target is removed. Hard links can't span file systems; symlinks can.

scenario: Which directory holds most system configuration files?
explanation: /etc holds system configuration files under the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard. /var is for changing data, /usr/bin for programs and /boot for boot files.

scenario: Where are log files usually stored?
explanation: Log files normally live in /var/log, because /var holds variable data such as logs, spools and caches. systemd also stores a binary journal that you read with journalctl.

scenario: Which command shows the type of a file's content, such as "ASCII text" or "PNG image"?
explanation: file inspects a file's content and reports its type, such as ASCII text or PNG image. Linux does not rely on file extensions, and type is a shell command for command names.

scenario: Which command finds every file named notes.txt under your home directory?
explanation: find ~ -name notes.txt walks the tree in real time and finds files by name. locate searches a prebuilt database (updated by updatedb), so it is faster but can be out of date; grep searches file contents.

scenario: Which command creates a gzip-compressed archive named site.tar.gz from the site directory?

options.note: gzip compresses files individually; it doesn't archive.

explanation: tar -czf creates (c) a gzip-compressed (z) archive file (f) from the named directory. -x extracts and -t lists, so tar -xzf would try to extract instead.

scenario: Which command lists the contents of backup.tar.gz without extracting it?
explanation: tar -tzf lists the contents of a gzip-compressed archive without extracting it. -x extracts, optionally into a directory with -C, and -c creates.

scenario: Which compression tool usually gives the smallest files of the three, at the cost of speed?

options.note: tar archives but doesn't compress by itself.

explanation: xz usually produces the smallest files but is the slowest, gzip is fastest and bzip2 is in between. tar itself only bundles and does not compress.

scenario: What does tar do on its own, without -z, -j, or -J?

options.text: Bundles files into a single archive without compressing them

explanation: By itself, tar bundles files into one archive (tape archive) without compressing. Compression is added with -z (gzip), -j (bzip2) or -J (xz), or by running a separate compressor.

scenario: What does > do in: ls /etc > list.txt?

options.text: Redirects standard output into list.txt, replacing its contents

explanation: > redirects standard output to a file and replaces its contents; >> appends, < supplies standard input from a file and 2> redirects errors. So ls /etc > list.txt overwrites list.txt.

scenario: How do you discard error messages from a command?
explanation: File descriptor 2 is standard error, so command 2> /dev/null discards error messages while normal output stays on screen. > /dev/null would discard stdout instead.

scenario: What does a pipe (|) do?

options.text: Sends one command's standard output to the next command's standard input
Runs commands only if the first succeeds

explanation: A pipe connects one command's standard output to the next command's standard input, as in ps aux | grep sshd. It doesn't run things in the background or write to a file.

scenario: Which command counts the lines in access.log?

options.note: Numbers lines but doesn't total them.

explanation: wc -l counts lines (-w words, -c bytes). There is no count or lines command, and cat -n only numbers lines.

scenario: Which command shows only lines containing "error" in app.log, ignoring case?
explanation: grep -i error app.log prints lines containing 'error' regardless of case. -v inverts the match, -c prints a count, and find does not search file contents.

scenario: In a regular expression, what does ^root match?

options.text: "root" at the start of a line
"root" at the end of a line

explanation: The ^ anchor matches the start of a line, so ^root matches 'root' only at the beginning. $ anchors the end, . matches one character and * repeats the previous item.

scenario: Which regular expression matches lines that are completely empty?
explanation: ^$ matches a line where the start is immediately followed by the end, i.e. an empty line. grep -v '^$' removes blank lines. $^ is backwards and ^.*$ matches every line.

scenario: Which pipeline lists unique login shells from /etc/passwd with how many users use each?

options.note: Uses the wrong delimiter (tab) and doesn't count.
uniq needs sorted input of the field first.

explanation: cut -d: -f7 extracts the shell field from /etc/passwd, sort groups identical values, and uniq -c counts them. uniq only merges adjacent duplicates, so sorting first is essential.

scenario: Which command shows the first 20 lines of a file?
explanation: head -n 20 prints the first 20 lines. tail prints the last lines, and tail -f follows a file as it grows, which is handy for logs.

scenario: Which command lets you scroll through a long file one page at a time and search with /?
explanation: less lets you scroll a file one page at a time and search with /; Space pages down, b pages up, n repeats the search and q quits. cat just dumps the whole file.

scenario: Which command replaces every "http:" with "https:" in links.txt and prints the result?

options.note: Reversed and only the first per line.
tr translates characters, and doesn't take a file argument.

explanation: sed 's/http:/https:/g' links.txt substitutes every 'http:' with 'https:' and prints the result; without the g flag only the first match per line changes. -i edits the file in place.

scenario: What is the first line of a Bash script, #!/bin/bash, called?

options.note: The kernel reads it to choose the interpreter.

explanation: The first line #!/bin/bash is the shebang: it tells the kernel which interpreter runs the script, such as /bin/bash or /usr/bin/env python3. It is not an ignored comment.

scenario: You wrote backup.sh. Which steps let you run it as ./backup.sh?

options.text: Add a shebang and run chmod +x backup.sh

options.note: Linux doesn't use extensions to decide.
Still needs execute permission or bash backup.sh.

explanation: Give the script a shebang and make it executable with chmod +x backup.sh, then run ./backup.sh (the ./ is needed because . usually isn't in PATH). bash backup.sh works without the execute bit.

scenario: Inside a script, what does $1 contain?

options.text: The first argument passed to the script

explanation: $1 is the first argument passed to the script. $@ holds all arguments, $# their count, $? the last exit status and $$ the script's PID.

scenario: What does an exit status of 0 mean?

options.note: Status is set when it ends.

explanation: Exit status 0 means success, and any nonzero value indicates a failure. Check it with echo $?, and && runs the next command only if the previous one succeeded.

scenario: Which test checks whether the file /etc/app.conf exists in a Bash if statement?
explanation: [ -f /etc/app.conf ] tests that a regular file exists. -d tests for a directory, -e any type, -r readable and -x executable, and the if block closes with fi. There is no 'exists' test.

scenario: Which test compares two strings for equality in Bash?

options.note: Missing $ so it compares the literal text "name".

explanation: Use = (or ==) for string comparison and -eq, -ne, -lt, -gt for numbers. Quote variables, as in [ "$name" = "admin" ], so empty values and spaces don't break the test.

scenario: What does this loop print? for n in 1 2 3; do echo "Item $n"; done

options.text: Item 1, Item 2, and Item 3 on separate lines

options.note: The loop runs once per word.

explanation: The for loop iterates over the words 1, 2 and 3, and "Item $n" expands the variable each time, so three lines print. It can also loop over globs or command output.

scenario: How do you store the output of the date command in a variable named today?
explanation: Command substitution $(date +%F) runs the command and inserts its output, so today=$(date +%F) stores the date. today=date stores the literal text, and spaces around = are not allowed.

scenario: Which command shows lines in file A that aren't identical to file B, line by line?

options.note: cmp reports the first differing byte.
Searches B for the text A.

explanation: diff compares two files line by line and shows the differences; diff -u gives the unified format used for patches. cmp compares byte by byte and comm compares sorted files.

scenario: Which command shows the running processes for all users?

options.note: jobs lists the current shell's jobs.
Lists /proc entries, not a process table.

explanation: ps aux lists every process for all users (a), including those without a terminal (x), with the owner shown (u). top and htop show processes interactively.

scenario: A program is frozen. Which command asks process 4321 to terminate gracefully?

options.note: SIGKILL can't be caught; use it only if SIGTERM fails.

explanation: kill 4321 sends SIGTERM (15), which asks the process to terminate gracefully. kill -9 sends SIGKILL, which cannot be caught and gives the process no cleanup, so try plain kill first.

scenario: Which command shows memory usage, including free memory and swap?
explanation: free -h shows total, used and free memory plus swap in human-readable units. df and du report disk space, not memory.

scenario: Which command shows how much space is free on each mounted file system?

options.note: du totals space used by files.
Lists block devices and filesystems, not free space usage.

explanation: df -h reports used and free space on each mounted file system in human-readable units. du -sh dir shows how much space a directory uses.

scenario: Which command lists block devices such as disks and partitions?
explanation: lsblk lists block devices such as disks and partitions as a tree with sizes and mount points. Disk names include /dev/sda (SATA/SCSI/USB), /dev/nvme0n1 (NVMe) and /dev/vda (virtual). lspci and lsusb list other hardware.

scenario: Which command shows kernel messages, such as a USB drive being detected?
explanation: dmesg reads the kernel ring buffer, and journalctl -k shows kernel messages from the systemd journal, so either shows a USB drive being detected. history and uname don't.

scenario: Which command shows the systemd journal entries for the sshd service?
explanation: journalctl -u sshd shows journal entries for the sshd unit. Add -f to follow, -b for this boot and --since to filter by time.

scenario: Which command checks whether the nginx service is running and shows recent log lines?
explanation: systemctl status nginx shows whether the service is active and its recent log lines. start, stop and restart control it, and enable sets it to start at boot.

refs.title: systemctl - Control the systemd system and service manager

scenario: How do you make the cups service start automatically at boot?
explanation: systemctl enable cups makes the service start at boot, while start only starts it now. enable --now does both.

refs.title: systemctl - Control the systemd system and service manager

scenario: Which command shows IP addresses on a modern Linux system?
explanation: ip addr (or ip a) shows IP addresses and is part of iproute2, the modern toolset. ifconfig, route and netstat belong to the older net-tools package.

scenario: Which command shows the default gateway?
explanation: ip route shows the routing table; the line starting 'default via' is the default gateway, for example default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0. ip addr shows addresses instead.

scenario: Which command lists listening TCP ports and the programs using them?
explanation: ss -tlnp lists listening (l) TCP (t) sockets numerically (n) with the owning process (p). Older systems use netstat -tlnp.

scenario: Which file contains the DNS servers a system uses?
explanation: /etc/resolv.conf lists the DNS servers the resolver uses. /etc/hosts is checked before DNS by default, as set in /etc/nsswitch.conf, and /etc/hostname holds the machine's name.

scenario: Which command tests DNS name resolution and shows the answer from the server?

options.note: ping resolves the name but isn't a DNS diagnostic.

explanation: dig (or host) queries DNS directly and shows the answer from the server. getent hosts name follows the system's full lookup order, including /etc/hosts. ping only tests connectivity.

scenario: Which component loads the Linux kernel when a computer starts?

options.note: systemd is started by the kernel as PID 1.

explanation: The bootloader, such as GRUB 2, loads the kernel. The boot order is firmware (BIOS/UEFI), bootloader, kernel with initramfs, systemd as PID 1, then services and login.

scenario: What is the process ID of systemd on most modern distributions?
explanation: systemd is PID 1, the first user-space process, and it becomes the parent of orphaned processes. The PID is 1 on every boot of a systemd system, not random.

scenario: What is the role of a device file such as /dev/sda?

options.text: It represents a hardware device so programs can access it like a file
It's a log of device errors
It's a backup of the disk

explanation: A device file such as /dev/sda represents hardware so programs can access it like a file. /proc and /sys are virtual file systems exposing kernel and hardware information.

scenario: Which command shows CPU details such as model and number of cores?
explanation: lscpu shows CPU details such as model and cores, as does /proc/cpuinfo. lsblk lists disks and free shows memory.

scenario: Which statement about installing Linux in the cloud is true?

options.text: Instances usually start from a prebuilt image; you choose a size, network, and SSH key instead of running an installer
You always boot an ISO installer

options.note: SSH keys are the default login.

options.text: Each instance needs a physical disk

explanation: Cloud instances start from prebuilt images, and you choose a size, network and SSH key instead of running an ISO installer. Configuration at first boot is handled by cloud-init.

scenario: Which command installs the tree package on Ubuntu?

options.note: dnf is for Fedora and RHEL.
rpm needs a package file and is for RPM systems.

explanation: sudo apt install tree uses apt, the package manager of Debian and Ubuntu. Fedora and RHEL use dnf, and openSUSE uses zypper; rpm -i doesn't resolve dependencies.

scenario: What does a package manager do that downloading programs by hand doesn't?

options.text: Resolves dependencies, verifies signatures, and tracks installed files for updates and removal

explanation: A package manager resolves dependencies, verifies signed packages from trusted repositories and records every installed file, so it can update and remove software cleanly. Manual downloads give none of that.

scenario: Which command shows the hostname and kernel version?
explanation: uname -a prints the kernel name, hostname, kernel release and architecture; uname -r shows only the kernel release. hostnamectl shows hostname and OS details on systemd systems.

scenario: A file shows -rw-r----- with owner alice and group finance. Who can read it?

options.text: alice and members of the finance group

options.note: The owner and group can read it; root can too.

explanation: The mode -rw-r----- gives the owner read/write, the group read only and others nothing, so alice and members of the finance group can read it. Everyone else cannot.

scenario: What octal mode gives the owner read/write/execute, the group read/execute, and others nothing?
explanation: Octal permissions add r=4, w=2, x=1: rwx is 7, r-x is 5 and --- is 0, so owner rwx, group r-x and others none is 750. 755 would let others read and execute.

scenario: Which command makes deploy.sh executable for its owner only?
explanation: chmod u+x adds execute for the owner (user) only. a+x gives everyone execute, chown changes ownership, and 444 removes write and execute.

scenario: Which command changes the owner of report.pdf to bob and the group to sales?
explanation: chown bob:sales report.pdf sets both owner and group, and needs root to give a file away. chgrp changes only the group, and chmod changes permissions, not ownership.

scenario: What does execute permission mean on a directory?

options.text: You can enter it and access files inside it by name
You can run every file in it
options.note: Files need their own x bit.
Deleting needs write on the parent.

explanation: On a directory, execute means you can enter it and access files inside by name. Read lets you list names, and write lets you create or delete entries. It doesn't let you run every file.

scenario: Why is /tmp mode drwxrwxrwt?

options.text: Everyone can create files, but the sticky bit (t) lets users delete only their own files
t means the directory is temporary

explanation: /tmp is drwxrwxrwt: everyone can create files, but the sticky bit (t) lets users delete or rename only their own files. It's intentional, not a mistake.

scenario: What does the SUID bit on /usr/bin/passwd do?

options.text: The program runs with the file owner's (root's) privileges, so users can update /etc/shadow
It runs with the user's group only
It prevents anyone from running it

explanation: With SUID set, /usr/bin/passwd runs with its owner's (root's) privileges, so ordinary users can update /etc/shadow. SUID files show an s in the owner execute position and should be audited.

scenario: What does the SGID bit do on a shared project directory?

options.text: New files inside inherit the directory's group
Only the owner can delete files

explanation: SGID on a directory makes new files inherit the directory's group, which suits shared team folders (chmod g+s or 2770). It does not make files run as root or read-only.

scenario: Where are user account names, UIDs, home directories, and shells stored?
explanation: /etc/passwd stores account names, UIDs, GIDs, home directories and shells. It is world-readable but no longer holds password hashes; those are in /etc/shadow, readable only by root.

scenario: What UID does root have?
explanation: root has UID 0. Regular users usually start at 1000, and system accounts use lower UIDs, often with nologin shells.

scenario: Which command creates the user maria with a home directory?
explanation: useradd -m maria creates the user and a home directory; then set a password with passwd maria. Debian's adduser is an interactive wrapper around useradd.

scenario: Which command adds the existing user maria to the developers group without removing her other groups?

options.note: Without -a it replaces the supplementary groups.

explanation: usermod -aG developers maria appends the group without removing her others. Without -a, -G replaces her supplementary groups. She must log in again for it to apply.

scenario: Which command creates a new group named auditors?
explanation: groupadd auditors creates a new group, groupdel removes it, and getent group auditors shows its members.

scenario: Why use sudo instead of logging in as root?

options.text: It grants admin rights per command, logs who did what, and avoids sharing the root password

explanation: sudo grants administrative rights per command, logs who did what and avoids sharing the root password. Access comes from the sudo or wheel group or /etc/sudoers. su - switches users with that user's password.

refs.title: Sudo Manual: Execute commands as another user

scenario: Which command shows who is currently logged in?
explanation: who lists the users logged in now, and w adds what each is running. last shows login history and lastlog each user's most recent login. whoami shows only your own name.

scenario: Which command connects securely to server1 as user admin?
explanation: ssh admin@server1 opens an encrypted session, listening on TCP 22. Telnet, FTP and rsh send data including passwords in cleartext.

scenario: Which command copies report.pdf to the /tmp directory on server1 over SSH?
explanation: scp copies files over SSH, as in scp report.pdf admin@server1:/tmp/. sftp and rsync -e ssh also transfer securely; plain cp only works locally.

scenario: How do you set up key-based SSH login to server1?

options.text: Run ssh-keygen, then ssh-copy-id admin@server1 to add your public key to authorized_keys
Email your private key to the server admin

explanation: Run ssh-keygen to create a key pair and ssh-copy-id to add the public key to the server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. The private key stays on your computer, ideally protected by a passphrase.

scenario: ls -l shows a symbolic link as lrwxrwxrwx. What actually controls access through it?
explanation: Symbolic link permissions (lrwxrwxrwx) are ignored; access is decided by the permissions of the target file. ls -l displays links as name -> target.

scenario: Which directories hold files that every user can write to but only for temporary use?

options.note: Each user writes in their own home.

explanation: /tmp and /var/tmp are world-writable directories for temporary files. /tmp may be cleared at boot while /var/tmp survives reboots longer; /etc and /usr aren't writable by ordinary users.
